metaDescription: Five cordless track saws compared on brushless motors, rail fit, kickback protection, depth on the rail and battery platform for sheet goods.
expertTake: The Festool TSC 55 KSEB is the cordless track saw to buy if you cut sheet goods for a living and want kickback protection and a thin-kerf blade, and the WEN 20691 is the value pick that includes two batteries and a charger. Skip cordless track saws if you cut full sheets daily, because a corded saw never runs flat and costs less.
introParagraphs: A track saw is a plunge circular saw that rides an aluminium rail. The rail clamps or grips the sheet, the saw locks into a groove and the blade follows a straight, splinter-free line. For breaking down plywood, cabinet sides and long rips, it beats a free-hand circular saw and approaches a table saw.

Cordless versions trade a cord for batteries, and that changes the choice. The details that matter are motor type, how the saw seats on the rail, depth of cut on the rail, kickback protection and the battery platform. The five saws below are compared on those and on who each is really for.

products.name: Festool TSC 55 KSEB Basic Cordless Track Saw, Bare Tool
products.description:
The TSC 55 KSEB is a professional cordless track saw with a brushless EC-TEC motor, a sensor-based KickbackStop system that rapidly stops the blade to reduce kickback and a 1/16 inch thin-kerf blade. The listing puts depth of cut at about 2.13 inches.

The thin kerf is a quiet advantage on cordless saws, because less material removed means less battery drawn per cut. KickbackStop is the safety feature that matters when a saw binds in a rip. Compared with the Milwaukee in this guide it is more precise and carries a stronger safety system but costs far more.

Because it is a bare tool, you need Festool batteries and a charger, and the rail is extra. Check the rail length, since a 55 inch rail is too short for a full sheet crosscut. The thin kerf blade also means cleaner cuts in veneered plywood, where tear-out ruins the face.
products.bestFor: Professional cabinet makers who want precision, kickback protection and a thin kerf.
pros: Precise rail fit for splinter-free cuts
cons: Bare tool needs batteries and a rail

products.name: Milwaukee M18 FUEL 6-1/2 in Plunge Track Saw 2831-20
products.description:
The 2831-20 is a bare M18 FUEL plunge track saw with a POWERSTATE brushless motor, a variable speed dial for setting blade RPM, a vac port and dust bag and a quick locking blade change system. An adjustable cam system lets you dial in the fit to the track.

Adjustable track fit matters, because play between saw and rail wrecks accuracy. Variable speed lets you slow down for laminates and plastics. Compared with the Festool it lacks a kickback sensor but costs less and works with a huge battery platform, and compared with the WEN it is a bare tool.

If you already own M18 batteries, this is the strongest value here. Keep the base clean and the dust port clear. If you already own M18 batteries, you can start with the bare tool and add a rail later.
products.bestFor: Tradespeople already on the M18 platform who want brushless power and dust control.
pros: Variable speed dial for different materials
Cam system dials in the track fit
Fits the large M18 battery platform
cons: Bare tool needs batteries and a charger

products.name: Metabo HPT 36V MultiVolt 6-1/2 in Track Saw Kit C3606DPA
products.description:
The C3606DPA is a 36V MultiVolt kit weighing 9.7 pounds with an adjustable bevel from minus 1 to 46 degrees and a depth of cut over 2-1/2 inches. The maker says it delivers best-in-class cutting per amp hour with a brushless motor.

Weight is the practical advantage, since a track saw is lifted and set on a rail all day. The negative one degree bevel allows a slight undercut for tight joints. Compared with the Festool it is lighter on features and price, and compared with the WEN it offers a wider bevel range.

Because it uses a MultiVolt battery, check that your other tools share it. A kit includes what you need to start. Because it is light, it suits ladder work and trimming in tight spaces, though a long rail is still awkward.
products.bestFor: Remodelers who want a light saw with a wide bevel range and a ready kit.
pros: 9.7 pound body is easy to carry

products.name: Makita XPS01PTJ 18V X2 LXT Brushless Plunge Saw Kit
products.description:
The XPS01PTJ runs on two 18V LXT batteries for 36V, a brushless motor rated at 6,300 RPM, and automatic speed change technology that adjusts speed and torque during the cut. The kit includes 5.0Ah batteries and the maker claims 50 percent longer run time than brushed designs.

Two batteries mean more power but also more weight and cost. Automatic speed change helps keep a steady cut in dense stock. Compared with the Festool it is cheaper but lacks the thin kerf and kickback stop, and compared with the Metabo it is heavier.

The LXT platform is wide, so many owners already have batteries. Keep spare batteries charged, since two are needed per tool. The dual-battery design gives long runs, so keep one pair on charge while the other works.
products.bestFor: Makita owners who want dual-battery power and a complete kit.
pros: Automatic speed change adjusts to load

products.name: WEN 20691 6.5 in Cordless Track Saw, Two 4.0Ah Batteries
products.description:
WEN's 20691 is a brushless variable speed saw with dual 20V Max battery ports, two 4.0Ah batteries and a charger in the box. It rips boards up to 2.25 inches thick and makes 45 degree bevel cuts in boards up to 1.65 inches thick, and it works with WEN's CT9502 and CT9110 tracks and CT992F clamps.

A complete kit at a low cost is the draw. Compared with the Festool it lacks a kickback sensor and the precision, and compared with the Milwaukee it is cheaper and includes batteries. The WEN track ecosystem is smaller, so check rail compatibility.

It suits hobbyists and occasional sheet work. Keep spare batteries charged and keep the saw base clean. Check the track compatibility before buying extra rails, because the ecosystem differs from other brands.
products.bestFor: Hobbyists who want a complete cordless kit at a low cost.
pros: Kit includes two 4.0Ah batteries and a charger
Rips boards up to 2.25 inches thick
Compatible with WEN rails and clamps

buyingCriteria.explanation: All five saws use brushless motors, which waste less energy as heat and hold speed under load. The Festool adds a 1/16 inch thin kerf blade, which draws less per cut. Cordless track saws burn through batteries on thick stock, so plan on two batteries for a full day of sheet work. On a cordless saw, a thin kerf is more than a nicety: every millimetre of wood the blade does not remove is energy the battery does not spend, and over a day of rips that adds up to extra cuts per charge.

Play between saw and rail wrecks accuracy, so the Milwaukee adds an adjustable cam to dial in the track fit. The WEN works with its own CT9502 and CT9110 tracks. Check that the saw adjusts to the rail, and that the rail has a splinter strip. Check how the rail ends: a rail with an anti-slip strip on the underside holds the sheet without clamps on light cuts, while a bare aluminium rail slides on laminate and needs clamps every time.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Depth of cut on the rail
buyingCriteria.explanation: Depth on the rail is lower than free-hand. The Festool lists about 2.13 inches, the Metabo HPT over 2-1/2 inches and the WEN 2.25 inches at ninety degrees. For thick hardwood or doubled sheets, check the rail depth, not the free depth. Cut a scrap before you commit to a good sheet, because the first pass after you change a blade or adjust the track will show any play as a slight step in the cut line.

The Festool has a sensor-based KickbackStop that rapidly stops the blade to reduce kickback. Others rely on mechanical features. A binding saw is the biggest hazard in a rip, so favour protection if you cut long boards. Dust control matters in a shop and in a house, so look for a port that fits your vacuum hose and a bag for when you are out on a site without one.

A 55 inch rail is too short for a full sheet crosscut. Rails are often sold separately, so a kit price can mislead. Count the rail, clamps and connector when comparing cost. Think about transport: a track saw is light, but a rail is long, so check that the case or a rail bag fits your vehicle before you buy.

The Milwaukee uses M18, the Makita uses dual 18V LXT, the Metabo HPT uses 36V MultiVolt and the WEN uses 20V Max. A bare tool is only a bargain if you own the batteries. Buy into the platform you will keep. Battery size changes balance: a large pack makes the saw tail-heavy on the rail, while a compact pack keeps it nimble but cuts fewer feet per charge.

specDecoder.meaning: A motor without carbon brushes that runs cooler and holds speed under load. A thinner kerf is easier on the battery but needs a stiffer plate. Match the rail length to the sheets you cut most often.
The width of the cut. A thin kerf removes less material and draws less power. Check the depth on the rail, not the free depth. A fine-tooth blade gives cleaner edges but cuts more slowly.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Festool lists a 1/16 inch kerf.

specDecoder.meaning: The cutting depth when the saw rides on the rail. It is less than free-hand depth. A bevel past 45 degrees helps with scribe cuts. Variable speed helps with plastics and laminates.
A sensor system that stops the blade quickly when the saw binds. Test any kickback system by reading the manual on how it resets. Weight with batteries matters more than the bare tool weight.
A battery that switches between voltage levels for different tools. Check whether the batteries you own work with the saw. Check dust port size against your vacuum hose.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cut accuracy hardware
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at rail fit adjustment, kerf and bevel range. The Festool and Milwaukee lead on precision. Loose rail fit loses points. We started with the rail interface and cut quality hardware, because a track saw is only worth the money when the line is straight and clean. We also treated the ecosystem of rails and clamps as part of ownership.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We read for kickback protection and dust collection. The Festool stands out. Units with no stated protection lose points. We read each listing for kerf, depth on the rail and bevel range, and we noted when a spec referred to depth off the rail. Weight was weighed with batteries attached.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power and battery
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared motor type and battery systems. The Makita and Metabo stand out for dual or MultiVolt power. We noted battery cost. We looked at the box contents, since a bare tool and a kit are priced differently and a rail may not be included. Parts support was noted where listings named replacement strips and blades.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit and ecosystem
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at what is in the box, including batteries and rails. The WEN kit includes both. Bare tools lose points for hidden costs. We compared battery platforms, because the battery is the long-term cost and the one most buyers already own. Cut quality was inferred from rail fit and blade design.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared weights and bevel ranges. The Metabo HPT leads at 9.7 pounds. Dual-battery saws lose points for weight. We kept cost to relative tiers, since track saw kits move widely between sellers. Value reflects what a user must buy beyond the saw.

cards.label: Kit
cards.text: The WEN, Metabo HPT and Makita include batteries. They suit buyers starting a platform.

cards.label: Bare tool
cards.text: The Festool and Milwaukee are bare tools. They suit buyers who already own batteries.

howToChoose.note: Choose a kit if you have no batteries and a bare tool if you do.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A thin kerf, a splinter strip, a rail long enough and a good dust port. Sheet goods punish a loose rail fit.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Festool and Milwaukee are the best fits, with the WEN as a budget alternative.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cut sheet goods daily and want kickback protection. The Festool is that saw.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cut occasionally. The WEN kit does the job.

maintenance.task: Clean the saw base and rail
maintenance.why: Dust on the rail causes play and rough cuts. A soft brush clears dust from the guide groove. Check the blade bolt torque before heavy use.
A worn strip leaves a rough edge. Wipe the rail with a dry cloth, never oil, since oil stains plywood. Keep the rail clamps free of sawdust.
A dull blade burns and strains the battery. Check the plunge spring for smooth return. Store the saw upright on its base.
Heat shortens battery life. Keep spare blades in a case. Wipe the battery contacts with a dry cloth.
Play grows with use. Adjust the cam or guide. Inspect the dust port for clogs after cutting MDF. Replace a bent rail section.

faq.q: Are cordless track saws as good as corded?
faq.a: They are close for most work, but batteries limit runtime on thick stock. Corded saws never run flat. Most owners say the biggest change is the end of tear-out on plywood and melamine, which a free-hand saw cannot match. Owners often add a second rail section so one setup handles both ripping and crosscutting a full sheet.

faq.q: Do I need a track saw if I have a table saw?
faq.a: A track saw handles full sheets more safely than a table saw. It also breaks down plywood in a driveway. A rail on a sheet of foam board on the floor makes a solid cutting platform in a driveway without a bench. Keep a spare splinter strip in the case, since it wears faster than any other part.

A dull blade, a worn splinter strip or play in the rail fit. Replace the strip and adjust the track. Set the depth of cut to about a quarter inch below the material, because a deeper blade exposes more tooth and increases risk. Plunge slowly and let the blade reach speed before it touches the work.

Many are 55 inches, which is too short for a full sheet crosscut. Buy a longer rail or a connector. If a cut wanders, check that the saw is fully seated in the rail groove and that the rail did not slip. Dust bags fill quickly with MDF, so empty them often.

Use the blade size and arbor the maker specifies. A thin kerf blade draws less power. A blade for plywood has a high tooth count, while a rip blade has fewer teeth, so keep both on hand. Check your battery charge before starting a long rip, because a stall mid-cut can burn the edge.

It kicks less than a free-hand saw when set up correctly. Clamp the rail and keep hands clear. Because the saw rides a rail, you can make accurate repeat cuts by clamping a stop block at the end of the rail. A pair of clamps for the rail pays for itself on the first slick laminate.
